The House of Representatives is the only branch of government directly elected by American voters since its formation in 1789. In the very first Congress, there were only 65 representatives the number grew over time as new states joined the country and the population grew. But in 1911, Congress decided the House was getting too big. So they passed a law limiting the number of representatives to 435. Proportional representation, really the heart of the American Revolution, is where the census becomes vitally important. According to some scholars and historians, since the house's number 435 was developed only in the reapportionment act of 1924, there's no reason there can't be more representatives per state. All Congress would need to do, as it did in 1924, is decide on a good number and divide up the congressional districts accordingly. So, as an aside, one change people really might consider when discussing structural change in D.C. would be to enlarge the house, giving the more populous states more power. Still, even as is, direct biennial elections and the size of the membership, currently 435 voting representatives, have made the House receptive to a continual influx of new ideas and priorities that contribute to its long-standing reputation as the People's House. Benjamin Franklin, Pennsylvania delegate to the Constitutional Convention, summed up the desired balance. Quote, If a proportional representation takes place, the small states contend that their liberties will be in danger. If an equality of votes is to be put in its place, the large states say their money will be in danger. Northern delegates countered that slaves were property and should not be counted at all. The result was the notorious three-fifths compromise, where each enslaved person was counted as three-fifths of a free person. The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified after the Civil War, began to remedy this infamous compromise by ordering the census to fully count every male individual, regardless of skin color. All female citizens had to wait for the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. While the number of House members for each state is determined according to a statistical formula in federal law, each state is responsible for designing the shape of its district so long as it accords with various provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which seeks to protect racial minorities voting and representation rights, or used to, but it was gutted recently by the Supreme Court, giving gerrymandering free rein. The Speaker of the House political and parliamentary leader of that body is second in line to becoming President of the United States after the Vice President. The speaker's position has evolved considerably over time, originating in the British House of Commons during the 14th century when the speaker had allegiances to the legislative body as well as to the sovereign. In the 18th century, speakers served as party leaders and ministers of government. The American speakership has grown from being held by regional or party leaders into a powerful post with the authority to appoint members to house standing committees and the authority to control the flow of legislation to the floor. James Madison wrote, quote, under these reasonable limitations, the door of this part of the federal government is open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, whether young or old and without regard to poverty or wealth or to any particular profession of religious faith. Among the special duties mandated for the House of Representatives are that the House has the power to name the President in case of a tie in the Electoral College. This was the duty they were performing on January 6th when the Capitol was besieged. The Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach an official, and it makes the Senate the sole court for impeachment trials. The power of impeachment is limited to removal from office, but also provides a means by which a removed officer may be disqualified from holding future office. Fines and potential jail time for crimes committed in office are left to the courts. Congress has the power to provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States, that is, to declare war, to make rules conquering captures on land and water, to raise and support armies, Provide and maintain a navy, provide for calling forth the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions, et cetera. The framers of the Constitution denied the president authority to go to war unilaterally. For most of U.S. history, the Constitution's checks and balances worked, and more often than not, presidents sought the consent of Congress on war matters. Nevertheless, over time, the executive branch began to assume more and more power in declaring hostilities, fulfilling Madison's dire prediction to Jefferson that, quote, the executive is a branch of power most interested in war and most prone to it. Period, close quote. This power remains a matter of contention and debate since the President is also named Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States and of the militia of the several states when called into the actual service of the United States. The Constitution also mandates that all bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives, although the Senate may propose or concur with amendments as on other bills, then that no money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in consequence of appropriations made by law. Thus, the House is invested with the power of the purse. Following the maxim that since the house was more immediately representative of the people, the people were to hold the purse strings. The House of Representatives may determine the rules of its proceedings, punish its members for disorderly behavior, and with the concurrence of two-thirds of members expel a member. In practice, the most severe type of punishment is expulsion, requiring that two-thirds majority vote. censure and reprimand are imposed by a simple majority vote of the full house. Expulsion has traditionally been reserved for only the most reprehensible conduct or crimes, such as treasonable acts. Indeed, the first three individuals expelled from the house had taken up arms for the rebel confederacy during the Civil War. The House, along with the Senate, has vested in themselves in investigative powers, and the Supreme Court has determined that the framers intended for Congress to seek out information when crafting or reviewing legislation. Such investigations include the powerful tools of subpoena power and of being held in contempt of Congress. In the Federalist Number 52, James Madison of Virginia, who would become the first former House member to later serve as president, wrote, quote, as it is essential to liberty that the government in general should have a common interest with the people.
